Blase

blah-ZAY · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Blase is unimpressed or indifferent due to over-familiarity with something.

After his fifth trip to Paris, he'd grown almost blase about the Eiffel Tower.

Worked Example

The seasoned flight attendant stayed completely blase through a bumpy descent that had first-time flyers gripping their armrests.

Years of experience had made the bumpy descent feel routine to the attendant, producing a jaded lack of reaction -- exactly what blase describes.

How Blase Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

jaded

jaded: worn out on a pleasure and no longer moved by it; blase adds the air of being above caring

unimpressed

unimpressed: not moved by admiration or interest

Antonyms

awestruck

awestruck: filled with overwhelming wonder

How Strong Is It? — unmoved → blase → world-weary

unmoved vs. blase

unmoved vs. blase: Being unmoved just means not reacting emotionally in the moment; being blase describes a deeper unconcern built up from too much experience.

world-weary vs. blase

world-weary vs. blase: A blase person is unimpressed by one familiar thing; a world-weary person has grown dismissive of nearly everything.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Blase comes from the French verb blaser, 'to satiate or cloy' -- the idea of having had so much of something that it stops producing any reaction at all.

Where it comes from

Where it comes from: Blase is the French verb blaser, 'to satiate or cloy' -- to have had so much of something that it no longer stirs you at all. Where blaser itself came from before French is genuinely uncertain; one theory ties it to old Dutch or Flemish words for drinking to excess.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Blase specifically comes from too much exposure to something, distinct from this unit's Saturnine (a permanent gloomy temperament unrelated to experience) and Stolid (calm dependability, not jadedness).
